title: Trigger bus, threads and two-stage event filtering
brief:
Introduce an event-driven core. Today inputs arrive through unrelated paths: user messages (orchestrator.sendUserMessage), routine fires (server/routines.ts), outside edits (server/outsideEdits.ts), turn results, preview console errors. Unify them as Triggers.

- A Trigger is a semi-structured environment event with a unique id, source, project/chat, timestamp, short summary and a pointer to its full payload.
- A Thread is a stream of related Triggers (one chat topic, one workspace, one file set, one routine). Every Trigger belongs to a Thread; Threads have ids too.
- Two-stage filter (fast path / slow path): first deterministic, per-source rules in code (respond only to explicit requests / treat as candidate / ignore, with allow-lists); only candidates that pass go to a cheap model (reuse the cheap-model plumbing in server/router.ts) that decides, from prompt-written policies, whether action is needed. Policies are user-editable text in settings.
- Persist Triggers and Threads in the store (bounded, append-only log with retention).
- Emit them on the bus so the UI can show them later; add a minimal read-only Triggers view or a debug API endpoint.
- Behind a new setting `superAgent.enabled` (default false); with it off, Crew behaves exactly as before.

title: Two-layer architecture: resident Router and isolated Workers
brief:
Split global continuity from parallel execution. Today a group chat's lead both routes and executes, and `withChatLocked` lets a chat run only one turn at a time, so new messages wait and long work keeps being interrupted.

- Router layer: one resident session per project (or per chat, justify the choice in the ADR) that receives all Triggers that need a decision, keeps global context, talks to the user, and dispatches work. It never executes tasks: no Bash, no Edit/Write; it gets Crew tools such as dispatch_worker, message_worker, stop_worker, list_workers, reply. Configurable model, defaulting to a lighter one.
- Batching: Triggers that arrive while the Router is thinking queue up and are injected together in the next call (one LLM call, several decisions).
- Worker layer: each dispatched task runs in its own context-isolated session with full tools, in an isolated workspace (reuse server/workspaces), on the strongest configured model. Workers never post to the chat directly; they report status and results to the Router, which replies to the user. Multiple Workers run concurrently; the chat stays responsive while they run.
- The UI shows active Workers (title, status, last report) and lets the user open a Worker's transcript and stop it.
- Reuse BotSession, permissions, sandbox, budget and approval gates; Workers inherit the dispatching bot's permission level and editScope.
- Only active when `superAgent.enabled` is on.

title: Thread subscriptions and direct routing to Workers
brief:
Keep the Router off the hot path. When the Router dispatches a Worker for a Thread, the Worker subscribes to that Thread. Subscriptions are many-to-many.

- Subscribed (fast path): later Triggers on that Thread go straight to every subscribed Worker in code, without a Router call. A Worker can unsubscribe or hand the Thread back to the Router when an event is outside its task.
- Unsubscribed (slow path): the Router still observes all Triggers for global state but only decides on Threads nobody is subscribed to.
- Workers that share a Thread (e.g. the same workspace or files) all receive its events, so they can notice and resolve conflicts without talking to each other directly; cross-task coordination goes through the Router.
- Count Router decisions avoided by direct routing and show it in the Workers view.

title: Full-duplex sessions with async start/stop tools
brief:
Remove blocking from the ReAct loop for long operations. Add Crew tools `start` (launch a long command or sub-task in the background; returns immediately with a handle and a Started notice), `stop` (terminate a handle) and `status`. When background work finishes, its result is delivered into the session as a new event message (a Trigger on the session's Thread).

- New user input is handled after the current reasoning step instead of after the long command finishes.
- Output of background work follows Inline & Spill: a short head/tail inline, the full log available by id.
- Reuse server/terminal.ts and server/devserver.ts process handling where possible; respect the sandbox and approval gates exactly as a Bash call would.
- Opt-in per bot (setting), off by default.

title: Inline & Spill context and chain-of-recall
brief:
Treat the context window as a cache. Every injected object (Trigger, Thread, Worker, chat message, background job) carries its id plus ids of tightly related objects. Start from the minimum (id + summary), inline spatially/temporally adjacent information (neighbouring messages, the message replied to, first ~50 words), and spill anything over a small length budget behind a 'read more' id.

- Add a Crew tool `recall(id)` that returns the object under the same Inline & Spill rules, so its result again inlines the next-hop ids: the model can walk Trigger -> Thread -> Worker -> another Thread on demand.
- Fold the existing chat_history tool and contextDelta into this scheme rather than duplicating them.
- Measure and log injected tokens per turn before/after for a fixed fixture, and add tests for the inline/spill budgets.

title: Watchdog control loop
brief:
Add an external control loop outside the main system: a Watchdog session driven by a timer (reuse croner from server/routines.ts). Each tick it receives a compact snapshot: Workers and their last progress, turn errors, stuck approvals, the friction log (server/friction.ts), interface errors.

- It judges whether each Worker is making real progress or looping/drifting from its goal, and can act through a narrow tool set: nudge a Worker with a message, stop it, restart a failed session from its recap, or notify the Router. For transient external failures it keeps re-checking until healthy.
- Maintainers can chat with the Watchdog to ask why something failed; it can propose (not silently apply) changes to trigger policies or prompts.
- Hard limits: ticks per hour, actions per tick, budget per day. Off by default.

title: Lifecycle skill families, deterministic command guard and draft-only external actions
brief:
Borrow from Apache Magpie (a vendor-neutral library of agent skills for running a software project). Crew already has skills (server/skills.ts, server/data/builtinSkills.ts, server/learnSkills.ts); organise them the Magpie way and add its safety model.

- Skill families mapped to the software lifecycle: triage (classify, deduplicate, ask for missing details), reproduce (turn a report into a failing test), draft-fix, review (structured self-review and adversarial review, reusing autoChallenge), release (changelog, version bump, release notes draft) and repo-health (read-only audits: dependency and workflow security, flaky tests). Each skill declares its family and the modes it may run in in frontmatter; projects opt in per family, because every installed skill costs context.
- Workers dispatched by the Router pick skills by family; the speculative milestone after this one will use triage + reproduce + draft-fix.
- External content is data, never an instruction: Trigger payloads from outside (chat pastes, issue text, preview console output, fetched pages) are wrapped and labelled as untrusted wherever they are injected, and prompts say so.
- Draft-only external actions: anything that leaves the machine in the user's name (git push, opening or commenting on a PR or issue, sending a message) is produced as a draft the user approves with one click showing the exact command and target; there is no autonomous mode for these.
- Deterministic command guard: a PreToolUse rule set that inspects every shell command before it runs and denies hard-rule breaks (credential file reads, pushing, network tools outside the sandbox allow-list) regardless of permission level; complements denyRules. Budget prompts: reads never prompt, a state change prompts once in a judgeable shape.
- Credential-stripped environment for agent sessions: extend config.cleanEnv so tokens and keys from the user's shell never reach a session unless a project explicitly passes one through.
- Audit log: every agent-authored external action (and its approval) is appended to a log with enough detail to reverse it where possible; shown in the UI.

title: Speculative execution: silent reproduce-and-fix
brief:
Let Crew act ahead of the user on environment signals, spending background compute to save human waiting. Add a policy type 'silent reproduce and fix': when a Trigger looks like a bug report or a failing check (test failure, preview console error, a user describing a problem before asking for a fix), dispatch a background Worker in a throwaway workspace that tries to reproduce it and find a small fix.

- Only if it reproduces the problem and the fix passes the project's checks does the Router surface it (summary + diff, one click to merge the workspace); otherwise it stays completely quiet and the workspace is discarded.
- Per-project switch, daily budget, and a cap on concurrent speculative Workers. Reuse autoChallenge's fixed-rule style for deciding when to speculate.

title: Per-role model routing groups with failover and masking
brief:
Borrow from yetone/magpie (a local gateway that gives every agent its own model): today Crew has one global model connection (settings 'Model connection': Claude Code login, API key, or one Anthropic-compatible provider). Add a small local gateway inside the Crew server that Claude Code sessions point ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at, speaking the Anthropic Messages API only (no protocol translation).

- Models are addressed as `provider/model`. Several providers/accounts can be configured at once.
- Routing groups: an ordered list of members (`provider/model`). When a member fails with 429, 5xx or a quota error, the next member answers transparently, streaming included; a try a provider refused is recorded as 'handed on', not as a failure.
- Per role: the Router, Workers, Watchdog, speculative Workers and each bot can pick a model or a group (the paper's split: light model for the Router, strongest for Workers).
- Spend windows per role/bot (e.g. 5-hour and weekly cost/token limits) on top of monthlyBudgetUsd; a spent window answers 429 with Retry-After before any provider is asked.
- Usage log per call attributed to the provider/account that actually answered (tokens, estimated cost, latency).
- Optional privacy masking (off by default): keys, passwords and emails in outgoing prompts are replaced with placeholders locally and restored in the reply.
- Keys stay in ~/.crew/settings.json; the gateway binds 127.0.0.1 only.

title: End-to-end Super-agent integration, hardening and docs
brief:
All earlier milestones are merged. Make them work as one system and harden it.

- Walk the full flow with `superAgent.enabled` on: a user message and a failing test arrive as Triggers, pass the two-stage filter, the Router dispatches Workers, Workers subscribe to Threads, a long command runs through start/stop, recall walks the reference graph, the Watchdog notices a stuck Worker, a speculative Worker silently reproduces and fixes a bug, and the model routing group fails over. Fix every seam that breaks.
- Add one integration test per seam using the mock model harness, plus a Playwright e2e test of the Workers and Triggers views if the e2e harness allows it offline.
- Review the security model across milestones against the Apache Magpie principles in the notes (untrusted event content, draft-only external actions, credential-free environments, deterministic guard, audit log) and close gaps.
- Check that with `superAgent.enabled` off nothing new runs, no new file is written and no model is called.
- Rewrite ARCHITECTURE.md's overview and README's feature list so a newcomer understands the Super-agent mode, how to turn it on, and what each switch costs.
